items.answer: Design guideline is a statement about an interactive system that says what should or should not be done to make it usable, without saying how to implement it; it can be generic or particular to a system, and is only a starting point to be implemented and tested.

Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
Mixed reality (MR) is an immersive technology that is the same as augmented reality, in which digital content is overlaid on the view of reality and can be interacted with.

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

questions.question: Which pair of stages forms the design stages in the interactive system development lifecycle?
options: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and the code design stage
the implementation stage and the empirical usability evaluation stage
the requirement-gathering stage and the interface and interaction design stage
the prototyping stage and the early evaluation stage
questions.explanation: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design. The other pairs either name non-design stages or mix a design activity with a stage that is not itself a design stage.

questions.question: How is code design characterized in the interactive system development lifecycle?
options: a new design language created for immersive system development
a later implementation step performed after coded development
the same code design used in non-interactive software development
a special code design introduced by interactive system development
questions.explanation: Code design in interactive system development is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development, so it is not a special interactive-system design activity. A design language is a separate way of expressing design, not the code design itself.

data.text: The interactive system development lifecycle contains two design stages, the design-prototype-evaluate design stage and code design. The code-design stage is treated as ordinary software code design, the same as in any other non-interactive software development.
points: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.
Code design in the interactive system development lifecycle is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

questions.question: In interface and interaction design, what are the two central issues?
options: How to gather and how to approve a design
Where to start and how to express a design
Where to place and how to style a design
How to test and how to refine a design
questions.explanation: Interface and interaction design centers on where or how to begin the design process and on having a way to express the design so it can be developed further. Placement, styling, approval, and testing are related activities but not the two central design issues.

questions.question: Which pair can serve as starting points for interface and interaction design?
options: Code design and release checks as starting points
Creativity and guidelines as starting points
Hardware and performance tests as starting points
Prototypes and user tests as starting points
questions.explanation: A design can begin from creativity, such as intuition or domain knowledge, and/or from design guidelines. Prototypes, tests, hardware choices, code design, and release checks belong to later or different parts of development.

questions.question: How do generic design guidelines usually differ from product-specific guidelines?
options: They are usually fewer and cover broad high-level aspects
They are usually company-specific and cover micro aspects
They are usually larger in number and cover product aspects
They are usually more detailed and cover micro aspects
questions.explanation: Generic design guidelines tend to be small in number and address broad high-level matters, while product-specific guidelines tend to be numerous and address the micro details of a particular system or product.

questions.question: Why can a prototype be treated as a design language?
options: It is a way to stop brainstorming about ideas
It is a way to lock in the visual ideas
It is a way to express interface and interaction ideas
It is a way to replace code design with final ideas
questions.explanation: A prototype can serve as a design language because it gives a concrete way to express interface and interaction ideas. It does not replace code design, and it is not meant to end brainstorming or fix a final form.

data.text: Interface and interaction design for an immersive experience uses a design-prototype-evaluation cycle to incorporate user requirements. It then considers how to begin the design and how to express it. Creativity, experience, and guidelines provide starting points, while design languages, including prototypes, make design ideas explicit and refinable.
points: Immersive experience design uses a design-prototype-evaluation cycle to incorporate user requirements.
Interface and interaction design chooses a start and expression: creativity, intuition, expertise, experience, domain knowledge, or generic/specific guidelines.
A design language specifies a design; interface and code designs generally differ, and prototypes express interface ideas.

questions.question: Guidelines for reducing cybersickness in highly immersive systems are an example of what kind of design guidance?
options: VR-specific guidance
generic interactive guidance
AR-specific guidance
GUI-specific guidance
questions.explanation: Cybersickness guidelines are tied to the immersion conditions of virtual reality, so they are specific to VR-like immersive systems rather than generic guidance for all interactive systems. They may not fit AR because AR immersion differs from VR immersion.

questions.question: What is the degree of applicability of generic design guidelines to XR systems?
options: fully, not partly, applicable
partly, not mostly, applicable
specifically, not generically, applicable
mostly, not fully, applicable
questions.explanation: Generic design guidelines apply to any interactive system, including XR, but they are mostly rather than fully applicable to XR systems. They are therefore not fully applicable, barely applicable, or specifically rather than generically applicable.

questions.question: What kind of design guidance are Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules for XR interface design?
options: Generic GUI-origin rules that can apply to XR interfaces
GUI-only rules that can apply to XR interfaces
VR-origin rules that can apply to XR interfaces
detailed product specifications that can apply to XR interfaces
questions.explanation: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are generic design rules that began as guidance for graphical user interfaces and can be partly or fully applied to other interface types, including XR. They are not GUI-only, VR-origin, or detailed product specifications.

data.text: Design guidelines differ in how broadly they apply: VR cybersickness guidelines are specific, because VR and AR immersion differ, while generic guidelines apply to any interactive system but only partly to XR. Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a generic example, originally 1986 rules for GUIs that can partly or fully apply to XR systems.
points: VR-specific cybersickness guidelines usually apply to VR or immersive systems, but may not apply to AR systems.
Generic design guidelines apply to any interactive system, including XR systems, though not fully to XR systems.
Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are 1986 generic GUI rules that can be partly or fully applicable to XR systems.

questions.question: What does Shneiderman's first golden rule of interface design ask a designer to do?
options: Provide informative feedback
Strive for consistency
Reduce loading latency
Create immersive visual scenes
questions.explanation: The first golden rule is to strive for consistency. Providing feedback, reducing latency, and creating visual immersion are related design concerns, but they are not the first rule.

questions.question: Which concept is shown when the same elements and interactions are used for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances?
options: Real-time responsiveness
Internal consistency
Universal usability
Informative feedback
questions.explanation: Internal consistency means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across parts of a design and usage instances. Universal usability, responsiveness, and feedback address different design goals.

questions.question: When virtual elements and interactions are made to match the user's real-world experience, what design goal is being supported?
options: Universal usability
Internal consistency
Informative feedback
External consistency
questions.explanation: External or environmental consistency means virtual elements and interactions closely match real-world experience so prior knowledge transfers. Internal consistency is about using the same design elements within the system.

questions.question: What does designing for universal usability require in an XR system?
options: Providing familiar labels for different user categories
Providing facilities for different user categories
Providing consistent controls for different user categories
Providing faster interactions for different user categories
questions.explanation: Universal usability means providing facilities for different user categories, not merely adding consistency, familiarity, or speed for those categories.

questions.question: Why can menu-based options be preferable to hotkey options for some users?
options: They rely on recognition rather than recall
They rely on speed rather than recognition
They rely on immediate action rather than browsing
They rely on keyboard memory rather than visible options
questions.explanation: Menus can be preferable when users may not remember hotkey combinations because menus support recognition, whereas recall is a skilled task. Hotkeys can be faster for users who already know them.

data.text: Shneiderman's first two golden rules for interface and interaction design are consistency and universal usability. The first rule is consistency, split into internal consistency, which keeps task-related elements and interactions the same, and external consistency, which aligns the virtual world with real-world experience. The second rule is universal usability, meaning the system should support all user categories, and menu-based and hotkey options are contrasted as different ways of meeting user needs.
points: Shneiderman's first golden rule is consistency, with internal and external, or environmental, consistency.
Internal consistency uses the same, not separate, elements and interactions for the same task throughout.
External consistency means virtual elements and interactions closely match users' real-world experience so knowledge transfers.
Shneiderman's second golden rule is universal usability: provide facilities for all user categories, not only specific ones.
Menu options use recognition rather than skilled recall, while hotkeys can be faster for users avoiding menus.

questions.question: Which usable-design rule requires the system to respond to whatever the user does?
options: universal usability
informative feedback
error prevention
consistency
questions.explanation: Informative feedback requires the system to respond to each user action. Consistency, universal usability, and error prevention are separate design rules.

questions.question: While a task is running, what does a progress bar mainly tell the user?
options: the success of the save operation and the changed icon color
the prevented error and the simple message shown
the completion level and the remaining wait
the consistency of interface elements and their placement
questions.explanation: A progress bar shows how much of the task is completed and gives a sense of how much longer to wait. Save success, interface consistency, and error prevention are not the information a progress bar provides.

questions.question: To make a dialogue yield closure, how should task execution be organized?
options: into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback at the start of each group
into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback for the user's errors
into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback for the user's category
into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback at the end of each group
questions.explanation: Closure comes from structuring the task as beginning, middle, and end and giving feedback when each group ends, so the user feels the task was started, executed, and completed. Feedback at the start, for errors, or for user categories does not provide that closure.

data.text: Usable interface design depends on two related rules: informative feedback and task closure. Informative feedback responds to user actions, helping the user understand what the system is doing and whether an action succeeded. Task closure complements this by organizing tasks into beginning, middle, and end, with feedback at each group’s end, so the user experiences the task as started, executed, and completed.
points: The third usable-design rule is to provide informative feedback for every user action, showing progress or successful completion.
The fourth usable-design rule is to design dialogues to yield closure by organizing tasks into groups and giving feedback after each.

questions.question: Why should close and start controls for the same interface not be placed side by side?
options: to prevent the user from overloading short-term memory
to prevent the user from missing informative feedback
to prevent the user from choosing the wrong action
to prevent the user from losing control of the system
questions.explanation: Placing close and start side by side can lead to an accidental wrong choice. The concern is not primarily feedback, memory load, or general control.

questions.question: Why should error handling avoid complicated messages?
options: because complicated messages can reduce the user's sense of control
because complicated messages can exceed the short-term memory limit
because complicated messages can hide feedback about the task
because complicated messages can confuse and scare the user
questions.explanation: Error messages should be simple because complicated messages can confuse and scare the user. The other effects belong to other usability concerns, not the stated reason for simple error handling.

questions.question: What are undo and redo facilities primarily meant to support in a system?
options: to let the user remember actions later
to let the user reverse actions
to let the user complete actions faster
to let the user get feedback on actions
questions.explanation: Undo and redo are primarily reversal facilities, letting users move out of an erroneous situation. They are not mainly feedback, speed, or memory aids.

data.text: Two system design rules explain how to handle user mistakes. The fifth rule pairs error prevention with simple error handling: designs should reduce error rates and give clear messages when errors occur. The sixth rule makes mistakes easier to recover from by permitting easy reversal of actions, mainly through undo and redo.
points: The fifth system design rule is error prevention, keeping error rates low because user errors cannot be eliminated.
Error handling should give simple, easy-to-understand information instead of complicated messages that confuse and scare users.
The sixth system design rule permits easy action reversal, primarily through undo and redo facilities.

questions.question: What does feedback about a user's action mainly protect against under the keeping-users-in-control rule?
options: the user missing the end of a task sequence
the user feeling at a loss about the system's response
the user accidentally selecting a nearby wrong control
the user being unable to reverse an incorrect choice
questions.explanation: Under the control rule, feedback lets a lay user see that their interaction changed the system state and produced a result; without it, the user can feel at a loss. The other options describe error prevention, reversal, or task closure rather than the control problem.

questions.question: What does the short-term memory usability rule require a designer to do with the information a user must remember to operate an interface?
options: storing it in long-term memory before the task begins
keeping it within the five-to-nine chunk limit
reducing it to one fixed-size unit for every application
showing it as a progress indicator during the interaction
questions.explanation: The rule keeps required interaction information within the short-term memory range of five to nine chunks. Long-term memory is a different store, chunk size is not fixed, and a progress indicator is a feedback device rather than a memory-load control.

questions.question: Why can the eight generic usability rules be applied to an extended reality system?
options: because they replace the need for tracking hardware
because they are not tied to one product or system
because they define the correct input modality for VR
because they measure a user's physiological comfort during use
questions.explanation: The rules are generic enough to be analyzed for applicability to broad classes of interactive systems, including XR. They do not substitute for hardware, prescribe a single input modality, or measure comfort.

data.text: Two usability rules are examined: keeping users in control and reducing short-term memory load. The control rule concerns user feedback and awareness of system change, while the memory rule is grounded in short-term memory's five-to-nine-chunk limit and in what counts as a chunk. The eight generic rules are not tied to one product, so they can be assessed for broad interactive systems, including extended reality.
points: The keeping-users-in-control rule helps lay users feel in control, perceive state changes, and receive feedback, reducing loss and poor usability.
Human short-term memory is a non-permanent store that brings long-term information to aid day-to-day activities.
George Miller's 1956 seven-plus-or-minus-two rule says short-term memory holds five to nine chunks, so fewer underuses and more harms it.
The reducing-short-term-memory-load rule keeps interaction information between five and nine chunks, a chunk being a letter, word, sentence, or concept.
The eight generic usability rules are not product-specific; they can be assessed for broad interactive systems, including extended reality.

questions.question: Which familiar interaction style is closest to interaction in a non-immersive augmented reality setting?
options: Changes to system-related settings
Object selection and manipulation
Movement from one point to another
Touch and gesture
questions.explanation: Non-immersive augmented reality interaction resembles familiar touch and gesture interaction. Object selection, movement, and setting changes are not the familiar style indicated for non-immersive AR.

questions.question: What outcome is served by suitable interaction techniques in immersive virtual or mixed reality?
options: Lower memory load
Simplified setup
Standardized actions
Enhanced presence
questions.explanation: Suitable interaction techniques in immersive VR or MR are used to enhance presence. They are not primarily chosen to reduce memory load, simplify setup, or standardize actions.

questions.question: Which immersive interaction category is concerned with changing settings?
options: Touch interaction
System control
Navigation
Object interaction
questions.explanation: System control covers interactions used to change system-related settings. Object interaction handles selecting and manipulating virtual objects, navigation handles moving between points, and touch interaction is not the system-control category.

data.text: XR interaction differs between non-immersive and immersive settings: non-immersive AR uses familiar touch and gesture-like interactions, while immersive VR or MR uses specialized techniques. Those immersive techniques are organized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control. This organization helps design the experience properly and enhance presence.
points: AR interaction in non-immersive settings is similar to familiar touch and gesture interactions.
Immersive VR or MR experiences require specialized, suitable interaction techniques to design properly and enhance presence.
Immersive interaction is categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, with selection, movement, and setting changes.

items.title: Order Shneiderman's golden rules for usable system design
steps: Striving for internal and environmental consistency
Designing for universal usability across user categories
Providing informative feedback about system action and status
Designing dialogues that yield clear task closure
Offering error prevention and simple error handling
Permitting easy reversal of actions such as undo
Ensuring lay users feel in control of the system
Keeping required information within five to nine chunks

questions.question: Why might design guidelines for avoiding cybersickness in virtual reality not transfer directly to an augmented reality system?
questions.reference_answer: Such guidelines are specific to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important. An augmented reality system's immersion differs from that of a virtual reality system, and immersion is an objective, quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide. Therefore a guideline based on virtual reality immersion may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality.

questions.question: Why can Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules help in designing an extended reality system although they were originally developed mainly for graphical user interfaces?
questions.reference_answer: They are generic design rules applicable to any interactive system, and an extended reality system is a kind of interactive system. The rules are not specific to a particular product or system, so they can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems. Because they can be partly or fully applicable to other interfaces, they remain useful for extended reality despite their graphical user interface origin.

questions.question: How do internal consistency and external consistency differ as aspects of consistency in system design?
questions.reference_answer: Internal consistency means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than separate objects, elements, or interactions. External consistency means that elements and interactions in a virtual world should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge. The first is uniformity within the design; the second is alignment with the user's real-world knowledge so it can transfer to the virtual world.
